title: Quantum-Logic Tsetlin Machines: Interpretable Quantum Machine Learning with Commuting Projector Clauses
abstract: Tsetlin Machines (TMs) learn interpretable Boolean clauses using finite-state automata. We introduce the Quantum-Logic Tsetlin Machine (QL-TM), which replaces Boolean literals with quantum propositions represented by projectors while retaining classical include/exclude automata. Clauses are restricted to commuting measurement contexts and activate through the Born probability of their joint projector. We prove an exact reduction to ordinary Boolean TM clauses in diagonal computational-basis contexts and connect Pauli-projector clauses to stabilizer and syndrome semantics. Controlled experiments on Bell states, phase-flip syndromes, randomized 16-class stabilizer tasks, mixed literal pools, context-budget ablations, and finite-shot noise show that correct non-diagonal contexts recover physically meaningful clauses, while diagonal or wrong contexts lose the relevant phase/syndrome information. The context-budget results closely follow the predicted separability ladder 2^(b-k) as true stabilizer generators are removed. The contribution is a controlled bridge between Tsetlin clause learning and quantum logic, not a claim of quantum advantage.
summary: This paper introduces the Quantum-Logic Tsetlin Machine (QL-TM), an interpretable quantum machine learning model that extends classical TMs to use quantum projectors. It demonstrates that by restricting clauses to commuting contexts, the QL-TM can successfully learn and classify quantum correlations, recovering physically meaningful information that is lost in simpler, diagonal measurements.
main_problem: To develop an interpretable quantum machine learning model that generalizes classical Tsetlin Machines (TMs) by replacing Boolean literals with quantum projectors.
main_result: The Quantum-Logic Tsetlin Machine (QL-TM) successfully recovers physically meaningful quantum clauses, achieving high accuracy on tasks like Bell state classification, which fails when restricted to diagonal measurements.
method: The model uses a hybrid approach where classical finite-state automata select clauses, and clause activation is determined by the Born probability of the joint projector of quantum propositions.
model_or_system: The model operates on quantum states ($ho$) on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, using projectors ($P$) as literals and restricting clauses to commuting measurement contexts, linking the framework to stabilizer and syndrome semantics.
key_observables: Clause activation probability ($	ext{Tr}(ho C_j)$), classification accuracy, and performance degradation following the predicted $2^{b-k}$ separability ladder.
important_parameters: Noise levels (depolarizing $p$), number of shots, and the context-budget ratio ($b$ vs $k$).
main_assumptions: The model is not a quantum Turing machine; the joint activation $	ext{Tr}(ho  igotimes L_i)$ is not guaranteed to equal the product of marginals, requiring a lightweight training surrogate.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QL-TM pipeline, showing context advantage (non-diagonal vs. diagonal contexts), and demonstrating performance degradation following the predicted separability ladder.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the QL-TM, proves its reduction to classical TMs in diagonal bases, and then validates its capability through controlled experiments on Bell states, phase-flip syndromes, and randomized stabilizer tasks under varying noise and context constraints.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, theoretically grounded framework for interpreting quantum correlations using established classical learning paradigms, bridging quantum logic structures (like stabilizer codes) with machine learning interpretability.

Fig. 2. Minimal QL-TM update used in the experiments. Classical finite-state include/exclude automata are retained while Boolean literal truth values are replaced by projector Born probabilities within commuting contexts.
Fig. 3. Context advantage for TinyProjectorTsetlin. Non-diagonal QL contexts solve the tasks, while diagonal Z-only contexts lose the relevant phase/syndrome information.
